title: WHO Member States continue negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex
date_evidence:
# WHO Member States continue negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex

20 July 2026

News release

Geneva
key_claim: The seventh Intergovernmental Working Group meeting on the WHO Pandemic Agreement closed on 17 July 2026 without a finished Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex; an eighth meeting runs 14-18 September 2026, and finalising the annex is a precondition for countries considering signature and ratification.
frame_summary: WHO argues that pathogen sharing and benefit sharing belong together in one multilateral instrument, and that the annex is the gate through which the Pandemic Agreement becomes operative.
verbatim_quote: countries reaffirmed their commitment to developing a PABS system that enables the rapid sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential, while ensuring the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their use, including pandemic vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics
verbatim_list: The IGWG will hold its eighth meeting from 14-18 September 2026.

Finalizing the annex is a critical step toward enabling countries to consider the signature and ratification of the WHO Pandemic Agreement, strengthening global health security and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response for future generations.
notes: Establishes that the multilateral benefit-sharing rule is still unwritten while bilateral terms are being signed. quote_provenance below.

title: Human Rights Assessment of the 2025-2026 US Bilateral Health Agreements
key_claim: Across seven assessed agreements (Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Liberia, Uganda), six require governments to negotiate broad data-sharing arrangements, five reference unilateral specimen-sharing, and failure to provide access can trigger changes to planned assistance or discontinuation, putting between US$124 million over five years for Liberia and US$1.8 billion for Nigeria at risk.
frame_summary: HRW argues that these agreements substitute an extractive bilateral bargain for the multilateral benefit-sharing settlement embodied in the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Nagoya Protocol, and that the opacity of the texts is itself the governance failure.
verbatim_quote: This means that these countries are committing to provide the US with “specimens, samples, sequencing data, and any other associated data related to novel and emerging infectious diseases with epidemic or pandemic potential.”
verbatim_list: Six of the seven agreements require that governments negotiate broad data-sharing arrangements.

In all agreements, failure to provide this access can result in “changes to planned assistance and/or discontinuation of the agreement,” meaning if they fail to comply countries could lose anywhere from US $124 million over five years in the case of Liberia to $1.8 billion in the case of Nigeria for HIV, TB, malaria, maternal and child health, laboratory systems, clinical commodities, and health workforce support that populations depend on for life-sustaining care.

However, according to a leaked draft template of the agreement, the US can then share the specimen and data with up to ten “non-U.S. Government U.S. entities” with the capability to develop diagnostics or other medical countermeasures.
The average lifespan of these agreements ranges from five to ten years, while Rwanda’s is for twenty-five years.

The following is a detailed human rights assessment of the text of the bilateral health Memoranda of Understanding between the US and Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Liberia, and Uganda.
notes: Advocacy organisation, but the assessment is document-based legal analysis of the agreement texts; treated as institutional research and corroborated against ProPublica and African Business. quote_provenance below.

key_claim: As of 3 August 2026, 34 countries had signed MOUs governing spending between 2026 and 2030 totalling at least US$24.2 billion, roughly 40 percent of it to be funded by recipient governments; global health financing fell 21 percent from 2024 to 2025.
frame_summary: The CFR team argues that the binding constraint on these agreements is fiscal feasibility, testing whether recipient governments can actually meet co-financing benchmarks as US contributions taper.
verbatim_quote: So far, the 34 MOUs govern spending between 2026 and 2030 and total at least $24.2 billion, roughly 40% to be funded by the recipient governments over the next three to five years.
verbatim_list: The 34 countries that have signed MOUs as of August 3 face widely varying cofinancing provisions, raising questions about their capacity to meet spending benchmarks, achieve target health outcomes, and replace foreign assistance.
Overall, global health financing dropped 21% from 2024 to 2025, according to the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME).
Nigeria and Botswana pledged to fund some of the largest shares of MOU spending, 59% and 78%, respectively.
notes: Updated tracker; the 4 August 2026 dateline is the current revision. quote_provenance below.

title: "Digital Colonialism": U.S. Demands to Access Africans' Data Raise Privacy, Sovereignty Concerns
key_claim: Uganda's data agreement gives the US direct, real-time access to nine national health data systems for seven years, including its electronic medical records system, against up to US$1.7 billion over five years; Kenya agreed to seven years of health records for US$1.6 billion, two years longer than the funding runs.
frame_summary: Lerner and Barry-Jester argue that the decisive term in these deals is system-level access to identifiable health records, and that the mismatch between what is promised in aid and what is surrendered in data is the story rather than the aid totals.
verbatim_quote: In the Ugandan data deal, the U.S. will get direct, real-time access to nine of the nation’s health data systems for seven years, including the central repository that stores all of its health information, lab data, data collected by community health workers and, critically, its system for managing individuals’ electronic medical records.
verbatim_list: Officials in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Ghana have been so outraged by the demands that they rejected the initial deals.

As a condition for receiving $1.6 billion in aid, the Kenyan government agreed to provide access to seven years’ worth of health records — two years longer than the U.S. would provide financial support.
In Uganda, the U.S. will provide up to $1.7 billion over five years for global health security and the treatment and prevention of deadly conditions such as malaria, tuberculosis, HIV and polio.

In response to follow-up questions from ProPublica, spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the agreements “share only the same kinds of aggregated, de-identified data that has been shared and used for years in the fight against HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, and other diseases. All data sharing is consistent with each country’s laws and approvals. No personally identifiable information is being received or shared by the United States government.”
After blocking the deal for months, in May, the Kenyan court temporarily allowed implementation of the agreement to proceed while it considers the case.
The State Department declined to publicly release global aid and data-sharing agreements it has signed with more than 30 countries as part of its new approach.
notes: Carries the on-record US State Department position used in the Counter-Argument. quote_provenance below.

title: US aid-for-data deals meet African resistance
key_claim: Since December 2025 the US has signed MOUs worth around US$20.6 billion with more than 30 countries; 21 African countries have signed, while Ghana, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe have rejected or paused talks on data privacy and sovereignty grounds. Kenya's Court of Appeal lifted an interim block in May 2026 with a full ruling expected by October.
frame_summary: Clynch argues that health data is being treated as a strategic resource comparable to critical minerals, and that the decisive weakness on the African side is the absence of a collective bargaining position rather than the absence of legal objections.
verbatim_quote: As with the Kenya deal, these MOUs involve governments accepting five years of funding in return for commitments to provide up to 25 years of patient data and disease pathogens.
verbatim_list: So far 21 African countries have signed such deals under the America First Global Health Strategy, including Nigeria, the DRC, Ethiopia and Uganda.
Indeed, since December 2025 the US government has signed memorandums of understanding (MOUs) worth around $20.6bn with more than 30 countries around the world.
Ghana, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe have all rejected the deal or paused talks, citing concerns over data privacy and sovereignty.
In May 2026, however, Kenya’s Court of Appeal lifted the restrictions on the agreement, with a full ruling expected by October.
According to Germany’s development agency GIZ, only 2% of global AI training data comes from Africa.
notes: Regional publication supplying the African-side voice, including the Zimbabwean government statement on reciprocity. Topic is anchored in Anglophone Africa, so the regional primary-source requirement is met in English; no Portuguese-language Mozambican or Amharic Ethiopian source was added. quote_provenance below.
